content:
- Overestimate prices after recent spikes, especially when sentiment is positive or neutral; model tends to overshoot and fail to correct downward quickly.
- Underestimate sharp drops or “sudden crashes” when sentiment turns negative or volatile; model is slow to react to negative sentiment signals.
- When sentiment is consistently negative over recent days, model should reduce forecasted price by 5–15% relative to prior peak, even if historical trend suggests continuation.
- If true outcome shows a sharp reversal from a recent high (e.g., 45→34), model should adjust downward by at least 10–20% in next 5–7 days, regardless of historical mean.
- Model overfits to recent high prices when sentiment is mixed or neutral; should apply mean reversion bias if 3–5 consecutive days show no significant change.
- When sentiment is positive but price drops sharply (e.g., +10% then -20%), model should not assume continuation of trend; apply “sentiment decay” rule: reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 3–5 days.
- If true outcome is below 30% of recent 10-day high, model should trigger “low volatility correction” — reduce forecast by 5–10% for next 7 days, even if sentiment is positive.
- Model tends to ignore sentiment shifts in early days of a new event; if sentiment changes direction within 3 days, adjust forecast by 5–15% in next 5–7 days.
